title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook  Standards and Templates
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines Redwood Inference's standard incident lifecycle, runbook structure, postmortem expectations, on-call rotation and escalation policies, game-day program, and standardized status page / customer communications templates. It is intended for all engineering teams (serving runtime, infra, SRE, platform) and for customer-facing teammates referencing operational state during incidents.

Goals:
- Provide a single, company-wide incident taxonomy and lifecycle that enables fast and consistent incident handling.
- Standardize runbooks so responders can act quickly with minimal context-switching.
- Ensure postmortems capture root cause and corrective actions and feed prioritized work back into product and engineering roadmaps.
- Maintain clear escalation and ownership so incidents are resolved within SLOs and communicated clearly to customers.

Scope and Audience:
- Applies to Redwood-hosted services (API, Console, Dedicated control plane), customer-facing infrastructure components, and private deployment support when Redwood is on-call.
- Audience: on-call engineers, incident commanders (ICs), support/CS escalation engineers, product owners, and engineering managers.

1) Incident severity taxonomy and SLO thresholds
- Sev 1 (Critical / P0): Total or near-total outage of a production customer-facing capability (e.g., API unavailable, severe latency degradation for >50% of requests, data corruption). Expected response: immediate paging, IC assigned within 5 minutes, mitigation within 1 hour where possible.
- Sev 2 (High / P1): Degraded behavior impacting a subset of customers or non-critical routes (e.g., elevated error rate >5% for >15 min for key endpoints). IC assigned within 15 minutes.
- Sev 3 (Medium / P2): Functional regressions or intermittent errors with workarounds available, or non-urgent operational issues.
- Sev 4 (Low / P3): Minor configuration issues, non-production incidents, or informational alerts.

SLO examples (single table):
| Service | SLO (Availability) | Error budget | Alert threshold | Responsible team |
| API Gateway | 99.95% monthly | 0.05% | 5xx rate >1% for 5m | eng-serving-runtime |
| Embeddings service | 99.9% monthly | 0.1% | 4xx/5xx rate >0.5% for 10m | eng-platform |

Notes: SLOs are authoritative in the Service Catalog and monitored by dashboards under eng-platform/dashboards. Teams must reconcile local SLOs with these playbook targets.

2) Incident lifecycle (high-level steps)
1. Detection & Triage: Automated alert OR customer report comes in. Pager duty triggers on-call.
2. Acknowledge & Assign IC: On-call engineer acknowledges within the SLA for the severity and identifies whether an IC should be assigned.
3. Triage & Mitigate: IC runs relevant runbook(s), applies mitigation (traffic re-routing, temporary rollback, capacity increases, kill/replace instances).
4. Communicate: Post status updates to internal incident channel and public status page if customer-visible. Use templates below.
5. Resolve & Verify: Confirm service health has returned to baseline metrics for at least 15 continuous minutes.
6. Post-incident: Create a postmortem (see template) within 48 hours of resolution and schedule follow-ups for action items.

3) Roles & responsibilities
- First Responder (On-call): Acknowledge alerts, apply immediate mitigations, and escalate to IC if required.
- Incident Commander (IC): Owns coordination, external comms, and outcome. Assigns tasks and ensures runbooks are followed.
- Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): Provide deep diagnostics, execute complex mitigations.
- Communications Lead (optional): Crafts customer-facing messages and updates status page. Usually Support / CS for customer-impacting incidents.
- Engineering Manager: Tracks action items and ensures work is prioritized.

4) Runbook standards and template
Every production service must have a runbook that follows this structure (stored under eng-platform/runbooks):
- Runbook Title (Service / Route)
- Purpose and scope
- Owner and escalation contacts (primary, secondary, pager info)
- Detection signals (metrics, dashboards, log queries, alerting rules)
- Quick mitigation steps (1-3 step checklist for initial stabilization)
- Detailed troubleshooting steps (ordered, with CLI/SQL/SQL-like examples and log queries)
- Rollback and recovery procedures (how to revert changes or roll back deploys)
- Post-incident verification checks (exact dashboards/queries and expected values)
- Automations and runbook playbook links (runbooks should call automation runbooks when available)
- Change log / last updated date and runbook owner

Example quick mitigation checklist (API Gateway):
1. Check gateway error rate in the gateway-dashboard (last 15m).
2. If error rate > 1%, scale gateway pool by +25% using infra autoscaling command: 
   - CLI: infra scaling set pool/gateway --replicas <current * 1.25>
3. If scaling fails or errors persist, failover traffic to secondary region: network-route set --service api-gateway --target region-us-east-2-secondary
4. If failover is not possible, flip to degraded-mode routing (return 503 for non-critical routes) using routing policy: routing apply degraded-mode

5) Postmortem template and expectations
All Sev 1 and Sev 2 incidents require a postmortem. Sev 3 may require a lightweight postmortem at the discretion of the IC. Postmortems should be completed within 72 hours and include:
- Title, incident date/time window, severity
- Incident summary (one-paragraph)
- Impact (customers, traffic %, regions affected, examples)
- Timeline (ordered events with UTC timestamps)
- Root cause analysis (what happened, contributing factors)
- Immediate mitigations applied
- Long-term fixes (action items), owner, and ETA (must be triaged into roadmap within 2 weeks)
- Postmortem severity opinion (Was this preventable? What could have been done earlier?)
- Lessons learned and follow-up verification plan

Postmortem grading and review cadence:
- The IC or incident author assigns a postmortem owner. The author presents the postmortem in the weekly incident-review meeting for Sev 1s. Action items are tracked in Jira and linked back to the postmortem page.

6) On-call rotations and escalation policy
- Rotation model: primary on-call (7 days) + secondary on-call (7 days) for each critical service group. Escalations happen if alert is not acknowledged in 5 minutes (primary), 10 minutes (secondary), 20 minutes (pager-schedule escalates to engineering manager).
- On-call responsibilities: monitor assigned alerts, maintain runbook accuracy, attend one game-day per quarter.
- Handoff checklist for rotation changes:
  - Confirm scheduled coverage in PagerDuty and internal calendar.
  - Run smoke test for critical routes (API health check).
  - Ensure runbook contact info and escalation lists are up-to-date.

Escalation matrix (example):
| Condition | Primary | Secondary | Manager | SRE Lead |
| Unacknowledged > 5m | Notify | Escalate | - | - |
| Incident unresolved > 60m | IC assigned | Page | Notify Manager | Notify SRE Lead |

7) Game days and simulation exercises
- Purpose: validate runbooks, test automation, and exercise cross-team coordination.
- Cadence: each critical service performs a game day once per quarter. Company-wide disaster recovery exercise annually.
- Game day checklist: pre-game objectives, injection plan, metrics to monitor, observers, and a retro at the end.
- Sample scenario: primary region network partition - simulate region failure, validate failover routes and capacity, measure RTO and RPO.

8) Status page and customer communications templates
- Criteria for public status page updates: any customer-facing disruption (Sev 2+) or ongoing degradation expected to last >15 minutes. Minor internal incidents (Sev 3/4) are not posted publicly by default.

Status page update cadence:
- Initial: Within 15 minutes of IC assignment - brief statement of detection and that investigation is underway.
- Update: Every 30 minutes for ongoing incidents with customer impact, or sooner for materially new information.
- Resolved: Final update summarizing mitigation and next steps within 1 business day.

Public status update templates (short):
- Initial: "We are aware of an issue affecting [service_name] that may cause [impact_summary]. Our engineers are investigating and we will post updates here. Incident ID: [INC-YYYYMMDD-###]."
- Update: "Update [T+30m]: Engineers have identified [interim_findings] and implemented [mitigation]. We continue to monitor. Impact remains [scope]."
- Resolved: "Resolved: The issue affecting [service_name] has been mitigated at [time UTC]. Root cause analysis and next steps will be posted in a postmortem. We apologize for the disruption."

Customer email template (for high-impact or enterprise customers):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident [INC-YYYYMMDD-###] - [service_name] - [Resolved / Investigating]
Body:
- Summary: One-paragraph summary of impact.
- What we are doing: Short bullets of mitigation and ETA for next update.
- Workaround: If available, include steps customers can take.
- Contact: CS escalation contact and incident reference.

9) Tooling and observability integration
- Incident channels: Use dedicated Slack channel naming convention: #incident-[service]-YYYYMMDD-[id]. Link the runbook and postmortem in channel header.
- Pager duty: All critical services integrated with PagerDuty with on-call schedules mirrored from the on-call calendar.
- Dashboards: Link canonical dashboards (Grafana) in the runbook with the expected panel thresholds.
- Logging & traces: Include representative log queries and a distributed trace example in each runbook (e.g., trace id query for request path).

10) Metrics and KPIs for the incident program
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) target: < 5 min for Sev 1, < 15 min for Sev 2.
- Mean time to mitigate (MTTM) target: < 60 min for Sev 1 (mitigation), < 4 hours for Sev 2.
- Postmortem completion rate: 100% for Sev 1 / 2, 80% for Sev 3.
- Game-day pass rate: > 90% critical steps automated / validated per playbook.

11) Continuous improvement and governance
- Quarterly incident review meeting chaired by SRE lead to review Sev 1/2 postmortems, track action items, and identify systemic reliability investments.
- Runbooks should be reviewed at least every 6 months and after any incident where they were used.
- Action items from postmortems must be triaged into team backlogs within 14 days and tracked to completion.

Appendices
A. Quick-reference checklists (one-page)
- Sev 1 checklist: acknowledge -> assign IC -> apply quick mitigation -> open incident channel -> post status page -> escalations as needed.
- Escalation contacts (example): Primary on-call: pager (PD) + slack @primary_name; Secondary: pager (PD) + slack @secondary_name; Eng Manager on-call: manager_pager@example.com

B. Example incident timeline snippet (UTC)
- 2026-02-01T10:03Z - Alert: API 5xx rate spike (1.8%).
- 2026-02-01T10:06Z - On-call acknowledged. IC assigned.
- 2026-02-01T10:12Z - Mitigation: scaled gateway pool +30%. Error rate began declining.
- 2026-02-01T10:28Z - Traffic re-routed to secondary region for affected customers.
- 2026-02-01T11:05Z - Service metrics returned to normal; IC declared resolved at 11:10Z.

C. Contact list and escalation matrix (maintained separately): ensure the runbook references the canonical contacts doc and on-call schedules.

D. Templates and links
- Runbook template: eng-platform/runbooks/templates/runbook-template.md
- Postmortem template: eng-sre/postmortem-template.md
- Status page: status.redwood.example.com (internal staging and public URLs)

If you are publishing an update to this playbook, include the change summary and reviewer sign-off in the runbook header. For questions, contact the SRE lead (sre-lead@redwood.example.com) or the author.
